title: Frozen Squirrel Poop Tells a 700,000-Year-Old Story
summary:
Have you ever wondered what a squirrel ate for lunch... 700,000 years ago? Well, scientists just found out—by sniffing and studying frozen poop! Yes, you read that right. POOP! And it doesn't stink... until it thaws. Then it really, really stinks.

Miners in the Yukon (a cold part of Canada) were digging for gold. As they melted the frozen ground, they found old squirrel burrows—like underground homes. Inside were tunnels, food stashes, and even little bathrooms. And in those bathrooms: frozen poop pellets.

Scientists thawed 13 of these ancient poops. The oldest was nearly 700,000 years old! That's way before humans had smartphones. They pulled out DNA—the tiny instruction book inside living things. The DNA told them what the squirrels ate. It wasn't just nuts and seeds. They found bits of grass, willow, beetles, grasshoppers... and even mammoth and bison bones!

Wait, squirrels eating mammoths? Don't worry—they weren't hunting them. They were probably chewing on bones for calcium, like some squirrels do today. One scientist even watched a squirrel on his fence eating a bone.

But here's the biggest surprise: the ancient squirrels might not be the same species as the ones in the Yukon today. The oldest one is so different, it might be a brand-new species! Its closest relatives live in China now.

So next time you see a squirrel, remember: its great-great-great (many times) grandpa might have snacked on a mammoth bone. Cool, right?
why_it_matters: This story shows that even tiny things like squirrel poop can help scientists understand creatures that lived long, long ago.

background_read: Squirrels have lived on Earth for millions of years, long before humans invented phones or computers.
The Yukon is a cold part of Canada where frozen ground can keep old plants and animal remains safe for thousands of years.
Mammoths were huge, furry relatives of elephants that lived during the Ice Age, so finding bits of their bones in squirrel poop is a surprising clue about the past.
